extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and scientific method (philosophy/science students, critical thinkers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying and critiquing common logical fallacies in arguments and philosophical/scientific reasoning; explains the forms, disguises, and examples of each fallacy and how to detect them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of Ambiguous Terms (Equivocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A term is used in different senses in different parts of an argument so that premises seem to support the conclusion verbally but not really; the same word shifts meaning between premises and conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect shifts in the meanings of key terms across premises and conclusion. Examples given: 'influence of property' (confounding persuasive influence with coercive influence); 'theory' (proper sense = result of induction; vulgar sense = imaginative conjecture); 'the Church' (clergy vs whole body of believers); Cicero's use of 'laudabile' (admirable generally vs exclusively moral); Descartes' pronoun 'I' (will vs laws of nature); free-will uses of 'I' (volitions vs dispositions vs actions); 'Necessity' (certainty vs compulsion); 'Same' (sameness _specie_ vs sameness _numero_); 'Force' in the vis viva dispute (different measurable effects); 'Infinite' in Achilles paradox (infinite divisibility vs infinite duration); ambiguities of 'right' (a moral claim on others vs absence of duty on self). Guidance/anti-patterns: when a word which appears to be the same is shown to have incompatible senses, the apparent inference collapses; clarify and fix meaning before inferring; beware of concluding about facts from a shift in connotation rather than extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of Composition and Division
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistaking properties of parts for properties of the whole (composition), or properties of the whole for properties of the parts (division); the middle term is collective in one premise and distributive in the other (or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether quantification is collective or distributive in each premise. Examples: geometric misapplication ('A B C is an angle of a triangle; therefore A B C is equal to two right angles' when the collective/distributive sense is confused); 'great men' argument (if any one great man could be replaced, infer erroneously that all great men are dispensable); lottery reasoning (confusing 'no uncommon occurrence to some one or other' with 'no uncommon occurrence to a particular individual'); practical examples: spendthrift who can afford 'this or that' but not 'all of them together'; medical reasoning that ignores aggregate symptoms. Guidance: make explicit whether claims are about single members or the class as a whole; do not shift the scope between premises and conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitio Principii (Begging the Question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a premise that is identical to or depends on the conclusion (or can only be proved from the conclusion), thus making the argument circular; includes reasoning in a circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archbishop Whately's definition: the premise either appears the same as the conclusion, is proved from the conclusion, or is such as would naturally and properly be proved from the conclusion. Detection strategy: challenge the reasoner to prove their premises — if they can only be proved by assuming the conclusion, the argument is petitio principii. Disguises and common forms: presenting the proposition in abstract terms as proof of the same proposition in concrete language; using 'nature' or 'essence' to smuggle the conclusion into the premise; assuming as fixed an arbitrarily selected 'nature' or set of properties that then overrule contrary facts; relying on mutual coherence (a neat concatenation of doctrines) as if it were independent support; examples: many Stoic ethical arguments in Cicero's De Finibus; Plato's assertion that justice and wisdom 'must be something'; philosophical attempts to prove infinite divisibility by premises that already assume it; Euler's flawed proof about minus × minus; ethical writers who assume 'natural sentiments' and then label dissenters 'unhealthy'. Guidance: look for hidden assumptions that do the work of the conclusion; be careful of premises that are merely restatements or rephrasing of the conclusion in different language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning in a Circle (strong form of Petitio Principii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two (or more) propositions are proved reciprocally from each other so that each is supported only by the other(s), giving no independent foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs often under pressure when one is forced to supply 'reasons' that themselves depend on the disputed claim. Example given (Whately): mechanicians proving 'every particle gravitate equally' by circular appeals: heavier bodies have more particles because particles gravitate equally, and vice versa. Detection: ask for independent proof of any link in the chain; if each proof depends on another unproven proposition in the chain, the argument is circular. Remedy: require at least one premise with independent justification or empirical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question-begging Appellatives (Loaded/Evaluative Names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using laudatory or vituperative names as premises so that the name itself embeds the disputed conclusion (naming that assumes the thing to be proved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious when an argument's force relies on an evaluative label rather than independent reasons. Examples: calling a reform an 'innovation' as though novelty implies badness; using a term like 'cupiditas' which already implies vice to prove that certain desires are vices. Guidance: replace emotive or evaluative appellatives with neutral descriptions and test whether the argument still holds; avoid letting connotative force of a name substitute for evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of Paronymous Terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusing words of similar root or appearance (paronymous words) so that an argument equivocates on related but distinct terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for reasoning that treats differently derived forms as if they were the same concept. Example: conflating 'cupiditas' and 'cupidus' or similar paronymous confusions; such shifts can introduce question-begging or equivocation. Guidance: inspect morphological relatives and ensure the intended sense is consistent across premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori Fallacy / Natural Prejudice (Inconceivability → Impossibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that because one cannot conceive of something, it cannot exist or be true; privileging intuitions or imaginative limits as proof of metaphysical impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text illustrates this with arguments for infinite divisibility or the impossibility of a minimum thickness that rest on inability to imagine a minimum. Detection: distinguish between what is inconceivable to imagination and what is logically or empirically impossible. Remedy: seek independent argument or empirical test rather than relying on imaginative resistance; note that premises appealing to 'we cannot conceive' often beg for further justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking Mutual Coherency for Independent Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Trusting that because a system of propositions hangs together neatly (mutual coherence), it must be true, even though the system may lack any independent support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tendency to accept a strongly coherent chain of doctrines as adequate proof is highlighted as a root of circular reasoning and petitio principii. Examples: ethical systems that explain away counterexamples by labeling dissenters as 'unhealthy' perceptions; whole speculative systems that are internally consistent but rest on unproven assumptions. Guidance: require at least some independently supported premises or empirical anchors rather than relying solely on internal coherence.
